transcript: You've applied to hundreds of jobs. You've spent hours tailoring your resume, filling out applications, and answering the same questions over and over again. And after all that work, you're still barely getting interviews. And here's the most frustrating part. It's not your experience or qualifications. It is a handful of ré mistakes that are causing recruiters to reject your application before they truly read it in detail. Hi, I'm Kate Kers, your career strategist and your career bestie. And today I'm breaking down five ré mistakes that cost people interviews all the time, plus exactly how to fix them. Let's get into it. The first mistake and one of the biggest deal breakers recruiters see is that your resume reads like a job description instead of proof of value. Recruiters already have a general idea of what your responsibilities maybe were. What they're trying to figure out is what impact you made, what problems did you solve, what changed because you were there, and why should they hire you over someone else? So, if your bullet point says something like responsible for managing social media accounts, that tells a recruiter almost nothing. Now compare it to this. Increase social media engagement by 45% through implementing audience specific content strategies and optimizing posting schedules based on engagement analytics. That instantly feels stronger because it shows results, strategy, and impact. One of the easiest ways to improve your resume is to stop writing taskbased bullet points and start writing valuebased bullet points. Instead of asking yourself, what were my duties? Ask yourself what changed because I did this job. Even if you don't have huge numbers or metrics, you can still demonstrate value. Maybe you improved efficiency, reduced errors, trained staff, solved problems, supported customers, or improved organization. Those are the things employers actually care about. Now, if you're thinking, "Okay, Kate, my bullet points are pretty good." The next mistake may be hurting you before recruiters even get to those bullet points. Mistake number two is that your resume doesn't make your value obvious fast enough. The top third of your resume matters a lot. Recruiters spend seconds scanning résumés, not minutes. And within those first few seconds, they should immediately understand three things. What role you're targeting, what your strongest qualifications are, and why they should keep reading. This is where your headline, professional summary, and core competencies need to do some heavy lifting. And please don't waste that space with something like resultsdriven professional with a proven track record of success. That tells me absolutely nothing about you. Instead, use that space to position yourself clearly for the role you want. For example, if you're targeting project management roles, your summary should quickly communicate project scope, industries, leadership experience, system knowledge, and measurable outcomes. If you're targeting healthcare administration, I should immediately see the healthcare operations, compliance, patient services, leadership experience, and process improvement. This is what I mean when I say put what's going to pop on top. Your resume should not make recruiters dig to figure out why you're qualified. Your strongest and most relevant value should be obvious within seconds. Mistake number three is a huge one right now. Your resume sounds exactly like everyone else's. Job seeers have been flooded with terrible ATS advice and recruiters are now reading resumes that all sound the same. results driven, strategic thinker, dynamic professional, detail- oriented, strong communicator. The problem is that everyone says those things. So instead of claiming a skill, prove it. For example, don't tell me you're a strong communicator, show me that you trained 25 new employees, presented quarterly performance updates to executive leadership, or coordinated projects across multiple departments. Those accomplishments demonstrate communication skills far more effectively than simply writing strong communicator on your resume. The same principle applies to leadership, problem solving, project management, and pretty much every other skill employers are looking for. And yes, keywords still matter, but they should be woven naturally throughout your accomplishments and experience, not dumped into one giant keyword snowball at the top of your resume. That just sounds robotic and like everyone else. Now, if you've made it this far, the next mistake may actually be costing you more interviews than all the other combined. Mistake number four is that you're trying to tell your entire life story on one resume. Recruiters do not need every task from every position you've ever held. Your resume is not your autobiography. It's a marketing document. Your goal is not to include everything you've ever done. Your goal is to include the information that best supports you for the specific role you're targeting. One of the fastest ways to strengthen a resume is simply cutting clutter. Go through your resume line by line and ask yourself, does this help support me for this particular role? If the answer is no, consider removing it, shortening it, or moving it to an additional experience section. When résumés become overloaded, the strongest information often gets buried. Less is usually more. And finally, mistake number five. Your resume is trying too hard to look pretty. I know the Canva lovers are already coming for me and I am also one of them. But trust me, a resume with graphics, icons, charts, photos, multiple columns, text boxes everywhere in heavy design elements can create serious readability issues. Simple and clean always wins. Your resume should make it very easy for recruiters to quickly understand your qualifications, experience, and your values because recruiters are not hiring your template. They are hiring you. So, let's quickly recap the five mistakes. Number one, writing your resume like a job description. Number two, not making your value obvious fast enough. Number three, sounding like everyone else. title: It’s OK to “Lie” on Your Resume — If You Do It This Way
description:
Is it okay to lie on your resume?
Not exactly — but changing your job title on a resume can be the right move when done correctly.

Many companies use internal or vague job titles that don’t match what employers and recruiters search for. Translating your title to a market-recognized job title (like Project Manager, Analyst, or Coordinator) helps recruiters understand your experience in seconds.

What’s not okay?
Inflating your level, claiming skills you don’t have, or misrepresenting your experience. That will cost you interviews.

Rule of thumb:
If you can clearly explain the title change in an interview, it’s ethical and acceptable.
